k-1.x_notes: Six substantial problems, all boards printed actual size (1-inch triangle edges), clean header and footer, and one shared rule stated once. P1 mixes coverable shapes (hexagon, 2x2 rhombus, chevron) with impossible ones: the odd-area 3-triangle trapezoid, plus two even-area shapes that still cannot be covered, the side-2 triangle and the 8-triangle trapezoid with 5 up and 3 down. That puts the coloring obstruction at a concrete entry point. P2 asks for fewest greens on triangles of side 2, 3 and 4 (answers 2, 3, 4). P3 is find-all on the unit hexagon (2 ways) and the 2-1-1 hexagon (3 ways), with spare boards. P4 asks for fewest blocks using mixed pieces (e.g. the side-3 triangle takes 3 trapezoids). P5 is a real strategy game with blue blocks on strips and a hexagon (answers first, second, first, first, second). P6 finds all 6 tilings of the 1-2-2 hexagon and records them on 8 small drawing boards. Weaknesses: 'say why' expects writing from kindergartners; drawing tilings on small grids is hard for K; the footer has no id; P6 may be long for the youngest. Visually identical to Y.
k-1.y_notes: Same text as X. The page images differ only by imperceptible antialiasing, so the strengths and weaknesses are the same: six real, concrete, actual-size problems with good contrasting examples and a strategy game, with somewhat heavy 'say why' and drawing demands for K.
k-1.reason: The two K-1 packets are identical in text and, to the eye, in every diagram, so there is nothing to choose between them.

grades-2-3.x_notes: Strong development of kernel 1. P1 has four boards. The star is balanced and coverable, the side-3 triangle has odd area, the 3-4 trapezoid has even area with 7 up and 5 down so it fails, and the 2-1-1 hexagon is coverable. P2's boards with holes contrast well: E has two up-holes and fails; the bowtie F is balanced overall but each half is unbalanced; G has opposite-orientation holes and works. P3 asks for fewest greens on triangles of side 2-5 with a lower-bound explanation, the side-5 board continuing on the next page. P4 generalizes to sides 10 and 100. P5 shows chevrons never beat blues, with a comparison table. P6 asks the child to invent a connected 20-triangle board needing at least 6 greens (13 up and 7 down, feasible). P7 asks for the rule for two greens on the side-2 hexagon: one up and one down always works, which I checked for all placements. Boards are actual size with enough space. Weaknesses: frequent 'explain' demands for 2nd-3rd graders; page 4 is a bare continuation with no problem label; P4 and P5 share a page with modest writing space.
grades-2-3.y_notes: Byte-identical to X (same text and same page images), so it has the same strengths (correct, well-sequenced coloring-obstruction work with good contrasting boards and an invent-a-board task) and the same minor weaknesses.

grades-4-5.x_notes: Good sequence for kernel 2: all 6 tilings of the 1-2-2 hexagon, its flip graph (diameter 4), flip distances on the side-2 hexagon, ribbons, parity, counting all 20 tilings, then the 1-3-3 board (20 tilings via ribbons). I decoded the Problem 3 diagrams: A to B takes 3 flips, C to D 4, E to F 8, all well posed. The ribbon definition has a clear L/R key and a consistent worked example (LRRLR on a 1-2-3 board). Weaknesses: P4 says 'Start with any covering' and asks for a 4-flip round trip that never flips the same hexagon twice in a row. That is impossible from the two extreme coverings E and F, which each have only one flippable hexagon, and F is exactly what sits on the board after Problem 3. So a child following the page naturally can be stuck on a broken task. P6 asks the child to prove nobody can beat 'your answer' for E to F, which is false whenever their Problem 3 answer was not optimal. P5's definition is long to read. The spare-board counts (10 and 8 for 6 tilings) don't match the answer, though that is harmless.
grades-4-5.y_notes: Identical to X except two sentences, and both are fixes. P4 starts from covering A, which has 3 flippable hexagons and does admit a 4-flip round trip with no immediate repeat, so the task is solvable and the 5-flip and 7-flip parity questions follow cleanly. P6 asks the child to find the fewest flips from E to F (8) and prove no one can do better, which is a correctly posed optimum-and-proof problem. It keeps all of X's strengths and shares only the minor weaknesses (long ribbon text, mismatched spare boards).
grades-4-5.reason: The packets are the same apart from Problems 4 and 6. X's Problem 4 is unsolvable from the extreme coverings, including F, the one the child is likely to have just built, and its Problem 6 can ask the child to prove something false. Y words both correctly.

overall.reason: K-1 and grades 2-3 are identical, so the decision rests on grades 4-5. There, Y fixes a genuinely broken task in X (a 4-flip round trip from 'any covering', which is impossible from the two extreme coverings) and a lower-bound prompt that can ask children to prove something false. One small but real mathematical defect separates them, and it favors Y.
